Accidental Release Prevention and Emergency Response Policies

Radford Army Ammunition Plant (RFAAP) is a government-owned, contractor-operated facility located in Radford, Virginia. RFAAP is owned by the U.S. Department of the Army, and is currently operated under contract by BAE Systems, Ordnance Systems Inc. effective 1 July 2012. RFAAP has been in continuous operation since 1941. RFAAP maintains an accidental release prevention program that covers design, installation, operating procedures, maintenance, management of change, and employee training associated with the facilitys processes. RFAAP maintains 24/7 on-site security and fire services through a contractor located onsite, and coordinates with both the Montgomery and Pulaski County Local Emergency Planning Committees (LEPC) and the City of Radford to provide additional emergency response resources if needed. 

Regulated Substances at RFAAP

The primary operations at RFAAP are propellant manufacturing processes for both military and commercial purposes. In support of these operations, RFAAP maintains more than the threshold planning quantity of four regulated substances: nitric acid (Chemical Abstract Service [CAS] No. 7697-37-2), ethyl ether (60-29-7), ammonia (7664-41-7) and oleum (8014-95-7); therefore, RFAAP is subject to the requirements of the RMP Rule (40 CFR Part §68). As all of RFAAPs RMP-covered processes directly support, the facilitys primary activity is defined under North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) Code 32592 for Explosives Manufacturing.

RMP Covered Processes at RFAAP

The RMP covered processes at RFAAP as of the October 2025 5-year update are summarized as follows:
?	Ethyl ether in combined storage and manufacturing processes; these include the Solvent Recovery Distillation Facility (SRDF), Activated Carbon Recovery System (ACRS), solvents bulk storage, as well as smaller tankage located in Solvent Propellant Manufacturing buildings). Despite the geographical areas co

vered by these processes, these components are considered one single process of interconnected piping and vessels.
?	Ethyl ether in Transient Railcar Storage.
?	Ammonia in Bulk Tanks at the Acid Area and Associated Piping to the C-Line Nitrocellulose Area for use at the Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) unit.
?	Ammonia in Tankage and Piping at the D-Line Nitrocellulose Area for use at the SCR.
?	Ammonia in Tankage and Piping at the EWI/CWP for use at the SCR.
?	Nitric Acid in bulk storage at the Acid Area, satellite tankage at the C-Line and D-Line Nitrocellulose Areas, and all associated piping inclusive of transfer lines from the Nitric Acid Concentrator/Sulfuric Acid Concentrator (NAC/SAC). These are considered one single RMP-covered process of interconnected piping and vessels.
?	Nitric Acid and Oleum in Transient Railcar Storage.
?	Oleum in nitroglycerin mixed acid (NGMA) Tankage and Piping at the Nitroglycerin Area for use in the manufacturing process.
?	Oleum in bulk storage at the Acid Area and satellite tankage at both the C-Line and D-Line Nitrocellulose Areas, and all associated transfer piping. These are considered one single RMP- covered process of interconnected piping and vessels.

Five-Year Accident History

The five-year accident history was evaluated for this 2025 RMP update. For documentation purposes, RFAAPs onsite version of its RMP document summarizes and evaluates all release events associated with each covered process, regardless of severity (i.e., inclusive of minor leaks contained entirely within secondary containment and with no personnel exposure) on an ongoing basis in order to identify the occurrence of any events that trigger the RMP update requirements to the EPA,.All incidents of safety and environmental significance must be promptly reported to management and each incident is investigated.
During the 2020-2025 5-year accident history period covered by this current RMP update, no qualifying events were identified for any of RFAAP

s covered processes. Although in this time period, RFAAP did have an ether spill and several acid spills that were reportable to the National Response Center because they exceeded the applicable reportable quantity thresholds, none of these events resulted in either offsite damages to the public or the environment, or onsite injuries, deaths, or significant property damage.
 
Accidental Release Prevention Program

The following sections summarize the components of RFAAPs Accidental Release Prevention Program, as required under 40 CFR Part 68. In addition to RMP Program Level 3 processes, a number of processes at the facility are also subject to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) Process Safety Management (PSM) standard under 29 CFR §1910.119. Therefore, RFAAPs Accidental Release Prevention Program is tailored to assure compliance under both the RMP and PSM regulations.

Process Safety Information: RFAAP maintains records of safety information that describes the chemical hazards, operating parameters and equipment designs associated with all covered processes.

Process Hazard Analysis: RFAAPs Plant Protection Standard (PPS)  Process Hazard Analysis (PHA) and Engineering Standard OSI-PSM-PHA Process Hazard Analysis detail RFAAPs requirements for conducting both initial and updated PHAs in a manner compliant with 29 CFR §1910.119(e). All critical safety actions prompted by PHA recommendations are required to be completed prior to process startup, and non-critical items are required to be completed within the timeframe established by the PHA. The required PHA revalidation frequency is specified as at least every five years after completion of the initial PHA to ensure consistency with the as-built design. All covered process PHAs were initiated, and any past pending actions are to be completed by 12/31/2025. 

Operating Procedures: All operating procedures are available to all employees through the Document Control System, and the operators a

re routinely retrained on these procedures. Consistent with the requirements of 40 CFR Part §68.69(a)(1), the process operating procedures contain steps for each operating phase, inclusive of initial startup, normal operations, temporary operations, emergency shutdown, emergency operations, normal shutdown, and startup following a turnaround or emergency shutdown. RFAAPs operating procedures also include information on the operating limits of each process, inclusive of the consequences of deviation from these limits and the steps required to correct or avoid deviation. Procedures are subjected to a routine review and recertification to assure that the contained information is correct and up-to-date.

Training: RFAAP has a dedicated Training Department which serves as the central repository for the maintenance of training records for all plant personnel. RFAAPs Master Training Plan describes these training processes . Each employee involved in the operation of any process at RFAAP is trained on the applicable Operating Procedures. All training includes emphasis of the specific safety and health hazards associated with the equipment and chemicals involved, as well as emergency operation and safe work practices. Initial training for each operator consists of reading the procedure, and being instructed firsthand on process operations via a walkthrough with the procedure in-hand. Upon any procedure change, each operator is retrained using the same methods as described for initial training. Per Procedure for Document Control, change levels are assigned to the procedures upon revision; the degree of procedure change determines the extent of training required to implement the change (i.e., Read, Observe, Guided Performance, and Supervised Performance). If there are no changes to the procedure, each operator is retrained on the procedure annually as a refresher. The TrainingDepartment maintains a database of each employees required training, including the date of

the initial training, the date of the most recent training, and the date that the next refresher training is required.

Mechanical Integrity: RFAAP has established written procedures to ensure the ongoing integrity of process equipment and that employees are trained in conducing these maintenance activities. Additionally, the facility has an overarching Maintenance Plan which documents the Preventative Maintenance and Inspection System. The aspects of this plan satisfy the requirements of 40 CFR §68.73 for addressing the ongoing mechanical integrity of pressure vessels and storage tanks, piping systems, relief and vent systems and devices, emergency shutdown systems, controls, and pumps. The centralized planning and tracking system of the Preventative Maintenance (PM) system at RFAAP is Maximo, which is an asset management software platform used to track the frequency of PMs and the date that the PM is closed. In the event that a defect is observed during a PM and additional work is required, the defect is noted on the work order, the original PM is closed, and a PM Defect work order is issued to track the corrective action to completion.

Management of Change: Management of Change is addressed in PM-eMOC  Radford Army Ammunition PSM Program Document, and all requests for process changes regardless of size must be entered into the Electronic Configuration Control System - Change Request via the intranet. Additionally, Form DUP-9728  Level of Risk Assessment for Management of Change is used to determine the associated level of risk for a change.

The Plant Process Control Board (PPCB) is also a key component of RFAAPs overall Management of Change framework, and governs both process and non-process changes. The Management Manual - Plant Process Control Board (PPCB) documents this process and aids in ensuring that the applicable requirements of OSHA 29 CFR §1910.119, EPA 40 CFR Part §68, International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 9001 are met.
An additio

nal key Management of Change tool utilized at RFAAP is its computer-based Management of Change (eMOC) system that can be accessed through any plant computer with network access. In addition to providing a centralized source for accessing the current operating procedures and associated controlled documents, this system also tracks the review and approval process for the appropriate personnel prior to procedure change implementation.

Pre-startup Reviews: RFAAPs requirements and overall process for pre-startup safety reviews (PSSR) are documented on a checklist  Pre-Startup Safety Review, and also discussed in procedure for Process Hazard Analysis. Prior to start-up, a Pre-Startup Safety Review Checklist form  must be completed and reviewed. The associated checklist ensures that procedures are in place and adequate, a hazards review has been performed as appropriate, and training has been completed prior to startup.. Completed and approved checklist forms are retained, at  a minimum, until the next 5-year Process Hazard Analysis revalidation for the subject process is performed.
A pre-startup review is not only required at RFAAP upon start-up of a new process or upon modification of an existing process, but also following an incident that results in a production shutdown, significant equipment damage, or injury. Following such an event, an incident investigation is conducted and followed up by a management review. The root cause failure investigation results and associated corrective actions are evaluated by the PPCB team for most incidents, and additional corrective actions will be recommended if necessary. The PPCB may request a follow-up review be held prior to operation start-up to ensure critical corrective actions are completed before the startup can occur.

Incident Investigation: RFAAPs  Safety Incident Reporting & Investigation Requirements describes the reporting and investigation requirements for events involving explosions, motor vehicle incidents, seve

re storm or weather damage and spills with occupational injuries. Per this written procedure, the investigation team must be formed and the investigation started as soon as possible based on the class of the incident and the conditions surrounding the incident and affected area. RFAAPs Management Manual   Environmental Quality and Safety Incident Reporting additionally describes the process for incidents that are classified as environmental in nature and do not necessarily trigger the Safety incident requirements. All spills at RFAAP are required to be reported and investigated as Environmental events, even if the event is a nominal release entirely contained within secondary containment and without resulting in any health or safety impacts. Investigation of even minor events and near-misses is considered a means of identifying and addressing potential issues, and thereby preventing more significant events. The incident investigation report is reviewed with all affected personnel and all incident investigation reports are retained for a minimum of five years.

Employee Participation: 
The Employee Safety Committee is established at RFAAP to promote safety compliance at the Radford Army Ammunition Plant. Through this forum, employees are able to meet monthly to identify and discuss safety and health issues and propose recommendations to  the management team. Employee involvement in incident investigations and Process Hazard Analyses is also required at RFAAP. Per procedurre  Safety Incident Reporting and Investigation Requirements, all incident investigation teams are required to include employees representing Operations, Maintenance, and Wage Employees as core team members. The procedure for Process Hazard Analysis describes RFAAPs requirements for employee participation, as representatives from multiple functional areas are required to be on the team.

Contractors: All contractors, subcontractors and tenants at RFAAP are required to read and certify by signat

ure that they understand and will abide by the rules identified in the General Plant Rules for Contractors, Subcontractors, Tenants and Government Employees. Representatives from Safety, at a minimum, attend a Pre-Work meeting to ensure that this information is clearly communicated. The booklet includes information ranging from general safety procedures, such as ladder use and hot work, as well as facility-specific hazards.
Compliance Audits: RFAAP Environmental is responsible for initiating, conducting, and documenting the RMP Compliance Audits on a minimum of a 3-year cycle. Any identified deficiencies are documented in the associated report, and tracking-to-resolution of proposed corrective action will be documented and maintained onsite as required.
 
Emergency Response Program

The All Hazard Mitigation Plan is the one major plans utilized by RFAAP. The plan specifically addresses a wide range of scenarios and is a complilation of several plans into one. Specific sections are as follows:
-- Incident Response Plan 
-- Emergency Operation Center (EOC) Plan 
-- Crisis Communication Plan 
-- Community Risk Profile- Standards of Cover
-- COOP- Business Continuity Management (BCM Plan) 
-- Wildland Fire Mitigation Plan
-- Water System Emergency Response Plan (WSERP)
-- THRIA
-- Anti Terrorism (AT) Plan 
-- Spill Prevention Control and Countermeasure Plan (SPCC) 
-- Tenant Emergency Action Plans (EAPs) 

This plan describes procedures, event communication and personnel responsibilities in the event of a disaster, as RFAAP recognizes that the potential for a chemical release exists as secondary to a causative event, such as a natural event or act of terrorism. The All Hazard Mitigation Plan distinguishes between Area Disasters, which are limited to one area or section of the plant, and General Plant Disasters which involve plant-wide response. The planning and organization detailed in the plan allow for response to the most devastating possibility, but are flexible eno

ugh to permit its adaptation to recovery from any disaster of lesser magnitude.
In addition to the notification exercises, RFAAP annually performs various response drills with local and state agencies as well as periodic tabletop emergency response exercises. The RFAAP contracted responders are part of the county wide emergency response plan. The RFAAP fire department is auto dispatched by the county for emergencies off-site but near the facility, as well as all incidents on-site.

Planned Safety Improvements

There is a multi-year project to refurbish and improve the Acid Area Tank Farm, inclusive of strong nitric acid and oleum storage. This is in progress and will involve improvements/replacements to the legacy tankage as well as to the secondary containment dikes. This updated infrastructure will continue to support the Nitrocellulose Manufacturing Process. There are several projects in the planning stages to improve workplace safety and develop safer, more modernized processes.
